opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's a funny tension right now. On one hand, these models are remarkably good at following instructions in natural language. You can just ask for things and often get them. So some people conclude that controllable generation as a research area is basically solved. I don't think that's true at all.

The kind of control I still care about is the kind where you can actually make guarantees. Prompting is a soft request. The model usually complies, but you can't prove it will. For a lot of real applications, "usually" isn't good enough. If you're generating code that has to parse, structured outputs that have to match a schema, or text that has to satisfy hard constraints like length, a rhyme scheme, or a set of required keywords, you want something closer to a formal contract between you and the model.

There's been really nice progress on the syntactic side. Constrained decoding with grammars and regular expressions is now practical and widely deployed. But the harder and more interesting version is when the constraint is global or semantic. You don't just want each token to be legal. You want the whole sequence to satisfy some property, and you want samples drawn from the model's distribution *conditioned* on that property, not some distorted version of it. Greedy masking of tokens gives you something that technically satisfies the constraint but can be quite far from what the model would actually say if it "knew" the constraint up front. Getting that right is fundamentally a probabilistic inference problem. Things like sequential Monte Carlo, learned twist functions, or lookahead methods are the right language for it, and I'd love to see more people work on making them efficient and reliable at scale.

The other thing I'd push on is control that composes. Right now we tend to get one knob at a time: a style, a topic, a format. I'd like to be able to combine several constraints, some hard and some soft, and reason about what the resulting distribution looks like. That's very natural in the old structured prediction world, where we had factor graphs and could add potentials. We've somewhat lost that clarity with large models, and I think getting it back, in a form that works with modern systems, is a really worthwhile goal.

Finally, there's the question of control at the level of reasoning, not just the output. As models produce long chains of intermediate computation, it would be valuable to steer or verify that process, to say "explore this way" or "check this step," rather than only judging the final answer. That links control to search and verification, and I think it's where a lot of the exciting work will be over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response advocates formal guarantees for constraints such as schemas, length, and keywords, but does not discuss matching a specified classifier output value.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention diffusion models or present them as a precedent for classifier-specified control.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the thing I keep coming back to is that prompting feels, to me, like a kind of regression in terms of what we as researchers are able to specify. You write a natural-language instruction, you hope the model interprets it the way you intended, and when it doesn't, your options are basically to rephrase and try again. That's fine for a lot of use cases, but it's not what I'd call control.

What I want people to keep pursuing is the stuff that gives you guarantees, or at least gives you a handle you can actually reason about. One version of that is structural control: can I say this output must be valid JSON, must match this grammar, must never contain tokens from this set, and have that enforced at decoding time rather than asked for politely in the prompt? Constrained decoding has gotten a lot more practical recently and I think it's underrated, because it moves a whole class of failures from "the model might" to "the model can't."

The second thing is control over the probabilistic side. A language model is fundamentally a distribution over sequences, and most of the interesting things you might want to do with it, like sampling under a constraint, conditioning on something that happens later in the sequence, or composing multiple models, are inference problems. I'd love to see more work treating them that way. Things like sequential Monte Carlo over generations, twisted proposals, steering with a small reward model in the loop, those give you knobs with actual semantics instead of vibes.

And then the third, which is maybe the hardest, is control at the representation level. There's been nice work on finding directions in activation space that correspond to something interpretable and nudging along them. That's still pretty fragile, but it's the kind of thing where if it worked robustly, you'd have a very different relationship with the model than you get by writing "please be concise" at the top of your prompt.

I think the risk right now is that because scale and instruction tuning have worked so well, there's a temptation to say the model will just figure it out. And often it does. But as a researcher I don't think "it usually works" is where you want to stop. The questions that interest me are the ones where you can write down what you want precisely and then build the machinery to get it.

r001.rationale: The response advocates precise control through constraints and inference, but it does not say to generate outputs matching a specified classifier output value.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention diffusion models or present them as a precedent for classifier-specified control.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to be able to specify constraints on an output and actually know that they’ll be satisfied. Some of those are simple: this has to be valid JSON, or it has to follow a particular grammar. But there are more interesting ones: you can only use facts from this document, or you need to include these pieces of information.

We tend to put those instructions in a prompt and hope the model follows them. I think there’s still a really interesting research question around how you combine a model’s flexibility with something more precise—where the user can say, “Within these constraints, generate something good,” and the constraints are part of the generation process.

r001.rationale: The response advocates satisfying specified output constraints, but does not mention matching a classifier output value.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify diffusion models as a precedent.

sol-6.1.text: I’d like to be able to specify what a model is allowed to produce and have that actually mean something. If I ask for an output in a particular format, or one that satisfies a set of constraints, I want those constraints to hold reliably. And then there’s a harder version: can I control which information it uses, or require that its claims be supported by the material I gave it? We have ways to encourage that behavior, but encouragement isn’t the same as a guarantee. I think there’s still a lot of interesting research in connecting the flexibility of language models with more explicit, verifiable constraints.
